Objectives
➢ Recall the characteristics, advantages, and disadvantages of
  different programming paradigms.
➢ Distinguish between classes and objects, attributes and
  methods.
➢ Identify the key principles of object-oriented programming
  (OOP).
➢ Recognize several OOP languages.




                                                                 3

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Given a problem, how to:
   Design an algorithm for solving it
   Implement this algorithm as a computer program


  Needs of programming languages and paradigms




                                                     4

1. Programming paradigms
➢ A Programming paradigm:
   a fundamental style or approach to programming
   defines how developers structure code, manage data,
     and solve problems.
➢ Different Programming Paradigms:
    Linear Programming
    Structured/Procedural Programming
    Object Oriented Programming
    Logical programming
    …

                                                          5

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Linear Programming: we can have a sequence of steps
 that can be executed or interpreted one by one until the
 program is finished.




                                                        6

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Procedural Programming: we divide our instructions
 into smaller blocks of well-defined code. These code blocks
 are known as functions, where each function performs a
 specific task.




                                                               7

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Procedural Programming




                           8

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Benefits of Procedural Programming
 • Simplicity – easy to learn and code.
 • Easy testability – straightforward debugging.
 • Good for small projects – suitable for general-purpose
   tasks.
 • Accessible learning – many resources available.
 • …




                                                        9

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Limitations of Procedural Programming
   Weak data security – data is exposed to multiple
    procedures.
   Limited portability – code reuse across projects is
    difficult.
   Poor real-world modeling – prioritizes procedures over
    data and objects.
   …




                                                         10

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Object Oriented Programming: is Programs are
  structured around objects that interact to perform tasks.
       Object = Data + Method
    OOP emphasizes encapsulation, inheritance, and
      polymorphism to build reusable, modular, and flexible
      code.




                                                          11

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Benefits of OOP include:
   Reusability – inheritance enables code reuse.
   Productivity – faster development with libraries and
    reusable components.
   Clear Interfaces – encapsulation and message passing
    simplify system interaction.
   Flexibility – polymorphism allows adaptable and
    extensible code.
  …




                                                       12

1. Programming paradigms
➢ Limitations of OOP include:
   Less suited for algorithm-heavy tasks – OOP focuses on
    modeling data/objects rather than pure computation.
   More complex code structure – requires classes, objects,
    and hierarchies, which can be overkill for small projects.
   Potential overhead – large OOP systems may compile or
    run slower due to complexity and interdependencies.
   …

➢ POP (Procedural-Oriented Programming) vs OOP (Object-

2. OOP concepts
➢ Object-oriented modeling
   Object in the real world are related to us and each
    other.
   They can be modeled as software objects.




                                                          17

2. OOP concepts
➢ OOP (Object Oriented Programming)
   A programming approach which uses objects.
   When a program runs objects are created and work
    together to perform the program's tasks.




                                                       18

2. OOP concepts

                  Object: An entity, or thing
                  ➢ Real   world      object    (car,
                    computer, ..)
                  ➢ Concept (subject, meeting, ..)
                  ➢ Process (sorting a stack of
                    papers or comparing two
                    computers to measure their
                    performance)

2. OOP concepts
➢ Object: Object in the real world is represented by:
    Attributes: information about theirs states.
    Methods: their behaviors related to theirs states.
➢ Example




                                                          20

2. OOP concepts
➢ Attribute:
   An attribute of a class is an identified common state of
    all instances of this class (i.e. set of concrete objects).
   An attribute specifies all possible values that can be
    assigned as concrete state of these of objects.

    Each object maintains a private copy of each attribute
    value.




                                                                  21

2. OOP concepts
➢ Operation:
   An operation of a class is
    an identified common
    behavior of all instances
    of this class. The
    behavior operates on the
    class attributes and
    usually    derives      the
    change of a class’s state.




                                  22

2. OOP concepts
 ➢ Object Class: A class specifies the common attributes
   and methods of many individual objects all of the same
   kind.
 ➢ Class is used as the blueprint to create objects.




    Object

➢ Object vs Class

2. OOP concepts
➢ Message passing is the only way to interact with objects
   Objects communicate by sending messages.
   Objects respond to a message that is sent to them by
    performing some action.




                                                             26

2. OOP concepts
➢ Message Passing: The process by which an object:
   Sends data to other objects.
   Asks the other object to invoke the method.
➢ Method Calling:
   The object to which the message is addressed.
   The name of the method to perform.
   Any parameters needed by the method.

3. Principles of OOP
Abstraction
➢ Abstraction hides the detailed information about object.
➢ Abstraction is a view or representation of an object that
  includes only the most significant attributes.
➢ Class represents such an abstraction and is commonly
  referred to as an abstract data type (ADT).

3. Principles of OOP
Encapsulation:
➢ Mechanism       by     which    we
  integrate of data (attributes) and
  operations (method) into a unit or
  class.
➢ It restricts direct access to some
  of an object's components, which
  can prevent the accidental
  modification of data.
➢ Encapsulation helps to keep the
  data safe and hide the complexity
  from the user.
                                       31

3. Principles of OOP
Inheritance:
➢ Create new classes (derived
  classes) from existing classes
  (base classes)
➢ The derived class inherits the
  variables and functions of the
  base     class   and      adds
  additional ones.
➢ Provides the ability to re-use
  existing code.


                                   32

3. Principles of OOP
➢ Polymorphism:
   Ability    of a message to be
    processed in more than one form.
   It is a feature which same message
    can be sent to objects of several
    different classes, and each object
    can respond in a different way
    depending in its class.
   The same method can perform
    different functions depending on
    the object that it is acting upon.

1. Overview of .Net
➢ NET is a cross-platform technology for building various
 applications (web, mobile, desktop, games, IoT, etc.).
➢ Provides a consistent object-oriented environment for
 different types of applications.
➢ Supports multiple Microsoft programming languages: C#,
 Visual J#, Visual Basic, etc.

1. Overview of .Net
➢ .NET Framework → .NET Core → .NET Unified as the
  three eras.
    Framework Era (2002–2022): Windows-only, strong
     desktop/web support.
    Core Era (2016–2019): Cross-platform pivot, modular
     runtime, open-source.
    Modern Unified Era (2020–present): Annual releases,
     unified product line, alternating LTS (even versions)
     and STS (odd versions).
➢ Language Evolution: C# has advanced from version 1.0 to
  C# 14 in .NET 10.

3. C# Programming Language
➢ Namespaces: a logical container that organizes related
 classes, interfaces, and other types into groups.
   Namespace declaration
    o Organizes related types into a logical structure.

    o Prevents naming collisions.

    o Example: using System;

   Using directive
    o Allows access to types by simple names.

    o Avoids writing full namespace paths.

    o Example: using System.Collections.Generic; use
      List<T> instead of
      System.Collections.Generic.List<T>.                 23

➢ Console I/O
   Read characters from the console window:

    o Console.Read(): Reads a character from the keyboard

     character.
    o Console.ReadLine():  Read characters from the

3. C# Programming Language
➢ Unconditional jump Statements:
   break: breaks out of the switch block. It was used to
    "jump out" of a switch/loop statement.
   continue: breaks one iteration (in the loop), if a specified
    condition occurs, and continues with the next iteration
    in the loop.
   goto: jumps directly to the label.

   return: the end of the method returns control to where

    o That copy will be deleted at the end of the method

    o The value of the passed parameter does not change
      after the end of the method

   names that can be used in code.

4. Exception handling
➢ Exceptions are generated when the implicit assumptions
  made by your programming logic are violated.
➢ You should incorporate a systematic exception handling
  process in your methods.
➢ To facilitate this process, the .NET Framework makes use of
  structured exception handling through the try, catch, and
  finally code blocks.




                                                                65

4. Exception handling
➢ Errors:
   Syntax Error
   Runtime Error => Exception

   Logical Error
➢ C# uses exception catching technique to catch and handle
 errors that arise during program execution.
➢ When an exception occurs, the program will immediately
 stop and the CLR will find and check the program to catch
 the exception, if not found it will terminate the program.


                                                          66

4. Exception handling
➢ Two exception handling mechanisms:
   Try and catch: try…catch…finally

    o The try statement allows you to define a block of code
     to be tested for errors while it is being executed.
    o The catch statement allows you to define a block of
     code to be executed, if an error occurs in the try block.
    o The   finally statement lets you execute             code,
     after try...catch, regardless of the result:
   throw…


                                                                 67

4. Exception handling
➢ try ... catch … finally blocks
    Code that is wanted to monitor to catch exceptions - put
    it in the try block.
    If an exception occurs in that block, the program will
    not end but immediately jump to the catch block.
    The statement in the finally block is executed whether
    an exception occurs or not.




                                                                69

4. Exception handling
➢ Some properties of the exception objects:
   Message: string containing the error message content.

   StackTrace: string containing the program execution
    steps until an error occurs
   Source: contains the name of the failed application or
    object.




                                                             70

           Handles errors generated when type is mismatched with the array type.

           Handles errors generated from referencing a null object.

  5        System.DivideByZeroException
           Handles errors generated from dividing a dividend with zero.

  6        System.InvalidCastException
           Handles errors generated during typecasting.

  7        System.OutOfMemoryException
           Handles errors generated from insufficient free memory.

  8        System.StackOverflowException
           Handles errors generated from stack overflow.                                   76

TOPIC 3



Object Oriented Analysis
  and Design (OOAD)
KỸ THUẬT LẬP TRÌNH

                                        1

Learning Objectives
By the end of this topic, students will be able to:
➢ Analyze a problem from an object-oriented perspective.
➢ Identify candidate classes, attributes and methods.
➢ Identify relationships between classes.
➢ Represent the design using UML Class Diagrams.

1. Application development phases
               Requirements
                 Analysis

              Object oriented

              Implementation


                  Testing



               Maintenance


                                    4

1. Application development phases
➢ Requirements Analysis
   Identify and gather requirements from stakeholders.
   Define the system's functionality and constraints.
➢ System Design
   Establish the architecture of the system.
   Determine how the system will be structured and
    organized.
➢ Object Design
   Identify the objects and classes needed in the system.
   Define their attributes, methods, and relationships
    (such as inheritance and associations).
                                                          5

1. Application development phases
➢ Modeling
   Use UML diagrams (e.g., class diagrams, sequence
     diagrams) to visualize the design.
    Ensure all interactions and data flows are clearly
     mapped out.
➢ Implementation
    Translate the design into code using an object-oriented
     programming language.
    Ensure that the code adheres to the design
     specifications.


                                                           6

1. Application development phases
➢ Testing
   Validate the system against requirements.
   Test individual components (unit testing) and the
    system as a whole (integration testing).
➢ Maintenance
   Update and refine the system as needed.
   Fix any defects and adapt to any new requirements.




                                                         7

Content


          Application development phases


            Object-Oriented Development Process


          Exercises


                                                  8

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Problem → Object Classes → Design → UML → Code




                                                   9

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Elements of Object-Oriented System:
   Objects: An object is something that is exists within
    problem domain and can be identified by data (attribute)
    or behavior.
   Class: A class encapsulates the data and its behavior.
    Objects with similar meaning and purpose grouped
    together as class.
   Methods: Methods determine the behavior of a class. They
    are nothing more than an action that an object can
    perform.
   Message: A message is a function or procedure call from
    one object to another. They are information sent to objects
    to trigger methods. Essentially, a message is a function 10or

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Identify the objects and classes needed in the system.
    Analyzing     the system's requirements (requirement
     documents, user stories, ..)
    Identify Nouns: look for nouns in the description of the
     problem or system. Nouns often represent potential
     objects or classes.
    Determine Real-World Entities: Identify entities that the
     system will model, such as “Student“, “Subject“, …
    Define Responsibilities: For each potential class, define its
     responsibilities and purpose.
    Group Nouns into Classes and Objects.

                                                               11

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Define their attributes, methods, and relationships.
    Attributes represent the characteristics of a class.
    Methods define the actions the class can perform.
    Identify Relationships between Classes.
➢ Refine and Review: review design to ensure it aligns with the
  system’s requirements. Refining may involve merging or
  splitting classes, adding new methods, or adjusting
  relationships as needed.
➢ Apply Object-Oriented Principles.



                                                            12

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Relationships:
   Association:   Classes are related to each other. Ex.
    "Teacher" - "Course".
   Aggregation/Composition: Classes are composed of or
    aggregate other classes. Ex. "Classroom" - "Student".
   Dependency: a class depends on another class.
   Generalization/Inheritance.
   Specialization/Realization: a class implement a interface.




                                                           13

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Features of Object-Oriented System:
   Encapsulation
   Abstraction
   Inheritance
   Polymorphism




                                        14

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ UML - Unified Modeling Language
   is a unified modeling language used to represent systems.
    It is used to create drawings to describe the system design.
➢ Object Oriented Analysis and Design (OOAD) using UML
 includes the following components:
   View
   Diagram
   Notations
   Mechanisms



                                                              15

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ UML Notation for class


         Class name
                           Attributes, Methods should
                           be shown as visible name.
     - Attribute 1         - private access
     - Attribute 2
     - …                   # protected access

     + Method 1()          + public access
     + Method 2()
     +…



                                                        16

Notations in UML
➢ Attribute representation
 − attributeName : Type [= Default]
   attributeName follows the naming conventions of the
    installation language of the application.
   Type should be the basic data type in the implementation
    language.
➢ Method representation
   + perationName(parameters): returnType
   parameter: in|out|inout parameterName:Type[= Default]
➢ Static members: Underline the name of static members.
                                                           17

Notations in UML
➢ Example

        Class name

    - Attribute 1
    - Attribute 2
    - …

    + Method 1()
    + Method 2()
    +…



                     18

Notations in UML
➢ Denoting relationships




                           19

Notations in UML
➢ Type multiplicity:
   n: exactly n
   0..* or *: zero or more
   m..n: between m and n
   Default value is 1




                              20

Notations in UML
➢ Association




   Class A ‘uses’ objects of Class B and reverse.
   Typically Class A has attributes of Class B and reverse.

   Navigability is from A to B and B to A: A Class A object can
    access the Class B object(s) and reverse.
                                                               21

Notations in UML
➢ Association




                   22

Notations in UML
➢ Association:



   Class A ‘uses’ objects of Class B.

   Typically Class A has attributes of Class B.
   Navigability is from A to B: A Class A object can access the
    Class B object(s) but the reverse is not true – the Class B
    object doesn’t know about the Class A object.



                                                             23

Notations in UML
➢ Aggregation: Aggregation represents a weaker whole-part
 relationship.




   Object(s) of Class B 'belong to' Class A

   Implies reference from A to B
   Object of Class B retain an existence independent of
    Class A.
➢ Example

                                                       24

Notations in UML
➢ Composition: Composition represents a strong whole-part
  relationship.




➢ Composition is similar to aggregation but implies a much
  stronger belonging relationship i.e. Object(s) of Class B are
  'part of’ a Class A object.
➢ Much 'stronger' than aggregation in this case Class B objects
  are an integral part of Class A and in general objects of Class
  B never exist other than as part of Class A.

                                                              25

Notations in UML
➢ Dependency: Dependency means that one class temporarily
 depends on another.
   One-way relationship: a class depends on another class.




                                                              26

Notations in UML
➢ Generalization: Inheritance should represent a genuine is-a
 relationship.




   Aside from associations,    the other main modelling
    relationship is inheritance.
   Class A 'inherits' both the interface and implementation of
    Class B, though it may override implementation details
    and supplement both.


                                                            27

Notations in UML
➢ Realization: Realization is commonly used when a class
 implements an interface.
   Semantic relationship between interface and class to
    implement the implementation of services declared in
    interfaces.
   Interfaces are similar to inheritance however with
    interfaces only the interface is inherited. The methods
    defined by the interface must be implemented in every
    class that implements the interface. Interfaces can be
    represented using the <<interface>> keyword

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
Problem:
Xây dựng chương trình quản lý sinh viên đơn giản của một trường
đại học:
    Sinh viên có các thông tin: mã số, họ tên, giới tính, tổng số tín
     chỉ của khóa học (sum) dùng chung cho tất cả SV. Biết 1 SV học
     nhiều học phần (HP) và mỗi HP có một kết quả HP.
    Kết quả học phần có các thông tin: mã HP, tên HP, điểm trung
     bình, số tín chỉ.
➢ Chương trình thực hiện các chức năng sau:
    Thêm/xóa/sửa thông tin sinh viên và kết quả các học phần của
     SV.
    Tính điểm trung bình chung, trung bình tích lũy (≥ 5) của SV.
    Cho biết SV đủ điều kiện tốt nghiệp hay chưa? Điều kiện tốt
                                                                     32
     nghiệp là tổng số tín chỉ tích lũy ≥ tổng số tín chỉ của khóa học.

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
Step 1: Understand the Requirements
➢ What does the system manage?
        Sinh viên, Học phần, Điểm.
➢ Who is involved?
       Sinh viên, giảng viên (nhập điểm), admin.
➢ What are the key actions?
       Thêm/xóa/sửa, đăng ký môn, nhập điểm, tính điểm
trung bình chung, TB tích lũy.
➢ What data needs to be stored?
       MSSV, họ tên, giới tính, tổng số tín chỉ của khóa học, mã
HP, tên HP, điểm trung bình HP, số tín chỉ.
                                                             33

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Step 2: Identify Candidate Classes
   Look for important entities in the problem domain, not
        every noun should become a class => need to refine the
        candidates.
E.g
      Danh từ            Là lớp đối tượng?   Lý do
      Sinh viên          Có                  Có dữ liệu + hành vi riêng

                                                                            34
      trường đại học     Không               Là hệ thống bao trùm

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Step 3: Design
    A class should have clear responsibilities.

    What should this object be responsible for?
E.g.
➢ Một Sinh viên nên:
   • quản lý thông tin sinh viên;
   • tính điểm trung bình (calculateAvg()), TB tích lũy;
   • kiểm tra điều kiện tốt nghiệp (isEligibleForGraduation()).

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Step 3: Design
    Responsibility → Data + Behavior
E.g.
➢ Student:
   • Data:
     - studentId
     - fullName
     - gender
      - sum_crredits
   • Behavior:
     + calculateGPA()

     + isEligibleForGraduation()

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Step 3: Design
   Identify Attributes: Attributes represent the state or
    characteristics of an object.
E.g.
➢ Student:
   - studentId: string
   - fullName: string
   - gender: bool
   - sum_credits: short

    Identify Methods: Methods represent behavior.

      𝐺𝑃𝐴 =        σ𝑛
                    𝑖=1 𝐶𝑟𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑡_𝑆𝑖




                                                     38

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Step 3: Design
    Identify Relationships: How are the classes related?
➢ Relationships:
    Association means that two classes are related.
    Multiplicity: How many objects can participate in a
       relationship?
E.g.
    Student 1 ───── 0..* CourseResult
    Course 1 ───── * CourseResult

2. Object-Oriented Development Process
➢ Step 3: Design
   Identify Relationships: Apply Encapsulation - Keep data
    private and expose controlled behavior.
E.g.
➢ Student:
   - studentId

   - gender

Learning Objectives

                                            3

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Abstract data type = data type + operation performed on
 this type
   Every operation related to a data structure is grouped
    together.
   Only possible operation are provided in the type's
    definition.




                                                         4

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ A class is the blueprint from which individual objects are
  created.
➢ A class specifies the common attributes and operations of
  many individual objects all of the same kind.
➢ A class defines a new data type, whose values are objects:
    A class is a template for objects; it abstracts a set of
     objects.
    An object is an instance of a class; it concretes a class




                                                                 5

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Encapsulation: Prevents the code and data being randomly
 accessed by other code defined outside the class.
   Group data and operations performed on these data
    together in a class
   Hide details about the class implementation from the
    user.




                                                         6

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Visibility scope
    Scope determines the visibility of program elements
     with respect to other program elements.
    Given a class:
     o A private attribute or operation of an object is
       accessible by all others objects of the same class
     o A public attribute or operation of an object is
       accessible by all others objects.




                                                            7

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Class declaration: using the keyword class followed by the
  name of the class.
➢ A class encapsulates following members:
    Name
    Variables: declare the attributes of a class
    Methods: declare the operations of class
➢ The visibility scope of a class can be explicitly set by
  declaring an access modifier.




                                                           8

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Four visibility scopes are identified in term of access
 modifiers to limit the access to the attribute and the
 operation:
   public: Everywhere (free access)
   private: Inside class only (class access)
   protected: Class and derived classes (only with an
    inheritance relationship)
   internal: Same assembly (assembly access)




                                                        9

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Variable declaration: Variables in C# can be declared at the
  class level or inside methods.
    Instance variables (member variables): declared within a
     class + outside any method. Each object has its own
     copy.
    Class variables: declared within a class, outside any
     method, with the static keyword
    Local variables: declared inside methods, constructors
     or statement blocks. They are accessible only within the
     block where they are declared)


                                                             10

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Method declaration:
   Declaration: Specifies the name of the method, its
    return type and its formal parameters (if any)
   Implementation:
    o Specifies a collection of statements that are grouped
      together to perform an operation.
    o These statements are executed when a method is
      called.
    o It is through the implementation of the method that
      the state of an object is changed or accessed.


                                                          11

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Class declaration: using the keyword class followed by the
  name of the class.
➢ Creating class Properties:
    Variables hold the data that an instance of your class will
     manipulate.
    The private keyword ensures that these instance
     variables can be manipulated only by the code inside the
     class.
➢ Creating class Methods: methods define the behaviors of
  the class.


                                                               12

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ <access keyword>/<access modifier>: affect the scope of
 the code.
   private: it is only accessible from code within the same
    class.
   protected: it is accessed from code within the same
    class, and it’s derived classes.
   public: it is accessed by code in other classes.
   internal: it is accessed by code in classes within the
    same assembly.



                                                           14

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Declaring and Using Objects: An object is an instance of a
 class
   <class_name> <object_name> = new <class_name> ([values])


   An object variable is a reference type, not a value type:
    o The variable does not contain the object's data directly.

    o It contains the memory address of the object created on
      the Heap.
   Ex.
      Student s = new Student();

                                                                  17

1. Defining classes, objects
➢ Accessing Members
   Data:

      <object_name>.<variable>

   Methods:

     < object_name >.<method>([parameter_list])

   Ex.
      Student s = new Student();
      s.Set(i, n, m);
      Console.WriteLine(“diem cua sinh vien: {0}”, s._gpa);
                                                              18

2. Constructors and Destructors
➢ What is a Constructor?
       A special method used to initialize objects.
➢ Characteristics
    Same name as class
    No return type (not even void).
    Usually public.
    Can be overloaded (multiple constructors).
    Automatically executed when the object is created.




                                                          22

2. Constructors and Destructors
➢ Types of Constructors
   Default Constructor (No parameters)
   Parameterized Constructor
   Copy Constructors
➢ Default Constructor: Provided by the compiler if no
  constructor is defined.




                                                    23

2. Constructors and Destructors
➢ Destructor
   Used to release memory when an object is no longer
     needed.
➢ Characteristics
    Same name as class
    Preceded by a tilde ~.
    No return type, no parameters.
    Usually public.
    Called automatically by the Garbage Collector (GC).
➢ In modern C#, destructors are rarely used.

   Refers to the current instance of the object.
   Useful in scenarios:
    o Disambiguation:   Distinguishing between instance
      variables and parameters with the same name.
    o Method Chaining: Returning the current object.

5. Operator Overloading
➢ Purpose
    Allows user-defined classes to behave like built-in types.
    Makes code cleaner and more intuitive (e.g., s1 + s2
    instead of s1.Add(s2)).
➢ Syntax:
   public static <data-type> operator T (<data-type> operand1 [,..])
   { … }


    T: operator



                                                                       44

5. Operator Overloading
➢ Overloadable Operators
      No.                           Operator
       1    Unary: !, ~, ++, --
       2    Binary: +, -, *, /, %
       3    Comparison: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
